title: Injunction applications - how to actually get an ex-parte order
p1:
Want an injunction without giving the other side prior notice?

You may be able to get an ex-parte order. But there is one thing many applicants get wrong: urgency alone is not enough to convince a court.
p2:
An ex-parte injunction is a temporary court order granted without hearing the opposite party first.

The court does not grant it simply because someone claims they might suffer a loss. You must demonstrate why waiting for notice could defeat the very purpose of seeking protection.

That distinction can make or break your application.
p3:
So, what actually strengthens your application?

Show the court three things: a serious legal issue that needs examination, a real risk of harm if immediate protection is refused, and why that harm cannot adequately be repaired later.

But here is the practical insight: your evidence of urgency matters as much as your allegation of urgency.

Attach relevant documents, establish the immediate threat through specific facts, explain why notice could cause further harm, and disclose all material facts, including those that may not favour your case.

In India, Order XXXIX Rule 3 CPC generally requires the applicant to explain why notice should be dispensed with and to comply with post-order service and filing requirements.
conclusion: What do you think carries more weight in securing an ex-parte injunction: demonstrating urgency or producing convincing evidence of the immediate threat? Share your perspective.
